History

The percolator bong grew out of the plain water pipe once glassmakers learned to fuse extra chambers and arms inside the tube. The tree percolator, a central stem with branching hollow arms cut with slits, was one of the earliest percolator designs, and trade guides still describe it as the most universal percolator style, usually built with four to twelve arms. The idea is old in outline: breaking one large bubble into many small ones increases the surface where smoke meets water, which is the same diffusion principle used in laboratory glassware and aquarium air stones. Percolator bongs became widely sold in the 2000s and 2010s as glassblowing workshops competed on diffusion designs, adding honeycomb discs, showerheads, and matrix grids alongside the tree. The tree arm remains popular because it diffuses strongly while keeping the draw open. Over time the same basic form was copied, adapted, and refined by many makers, so the record today covers a family of closely related objects rather than a single patented shape. Trade guides and manufacturer manuals preserve the steps of that change. The history matters because it explains why the parts are arranged the way they are: each feature survives because it solved a practical problem for the people who used the supply every day. The form changed slowly, through small improvements in materials and manufacturing rather than sudden reinvention, and each improvement can be traced in the sources cited at the end of this record. What stayed constant was the job itself, and what changed was how reliably, how evenly, and how durably that job could be done with ordinary materials and ordinary tools.

The supply in detail

The percolator bong (tree/arm) works by smoke from the bowl is forced through a tree percolator of hollow branching arms, each cut with slits, so it breaks into many small bubble streams in the water before rising to the mouthpiece. It is made from signature borosilicate glass with reinforced arm roots; 12-arm tree percolator; glass downstem and bowl, and a common example measures 400 mm tall; tube 65 mm diameter; 12-arm tree percolator, each arm 45 mm long with 8 slits; water depth 55 mm. The parts fit together in a fixed order, and each part has one job: to hold the material, to apply the mechanism, or to carry the result to the user. Because the parts are simple and the mechanism is mechanical or thermal rather than electronic in its basic form, the supply can be understood by inspection, measured with a ruler, and checked by the arithmetic in this record. The variants listed in the specification show how makers change size, material, and detail while keeping the same working principle, and the scale variants at the end of this record show the same design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes.

Parts and variants

Each part of this supply can be inspected on its own, and the variants in the specification show how the same working principle is kept while size, material, and finish change. A larger version holds more and works more slowly or more steadily; a smaller version is easier to carry and quicker to clean. Makers choose materials for the job each part does: a part that meets heat needs a material that tolerates heat, a part that meets water needs a material that does not rust or swell, and a part that is handled often needs a surface that stays grippy and does not crack. The scale variants at the end of this record carry that same logic further, showing the design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes, so the reader can see which dimensions change with scale and which stay the same.

Spec

Materials: Signature borosilicate glass with reinforced arm roots; 12-arm tree percolator; glass downstem and bowl

Dimensions: 400 mm tall; tube 65 mm diameter; 12-arm tree percolator, each arm 45 mm long with 8 slits; water depth 55 mm

Mechanism: Grove perc: the Signature design thickens the root of each arm where it meets the central stem, so the arms resist snapping while keeping the same slit pattern

Use: Fill until the arms are covered, pack the bowl, draw slowly until the chamber fills, then clear

Care: Soak the percolator in isopropyl alcohol to clear the slits; rinse well; dry fully; handle gently

Variants: Pocket grove, standard grove, and workshop grove versions; arm count varies by variant

Materials and design

Borosilicate glass is chosen for the percolator because the arms must be blown thin and hollow and then cut with slits, and only a glass that tolerates heat and holds a fine edge will keep those slits open and even. The central stem carries the smoke down to the arms, and each arm is a hollow tube open at its slits, so the smoke has nowhere to go but out through the water. The joints are the same ground-glass tapers as on the beaker, 14 mm or 18 mm, sealing by friction with no gasket and no thread. The outside is left smooth and clear so the percolator can be seen working and the water level read at a glance.

Build it yourself

A percolator bong cannot be made at home: fusing a tree percolator with hollow slitted arms inside a glass tube is a skilled glassblowing trade, and no home method produces it safely. The closest genuine maker activity is assembling a bought kit and making a cleaning stand for it. Buy a percolator tube, a downstem, and a bowl in matching joint sizes, and check the fit dry before any water goes in: the downstem should seat firmly without wobble, and the water must cover the percolator arms when filled. Check the fit dry before any water or load goes in, and work slowly, because a build that is checked at each step is the one that works the first time it is used.

3D printing

A glass percolator bong is not 3D-printable at home: no home filament prints glass, and a printed plastic tube could not hold the fused tree percolator or seal to a glass downstem. Print time (estimate): 2 hours 50 minutes for the stand and 45 minutes for the holder, at the settings given. Unmodelled factors that change real print time and strength are wall thickness, supports, nozzle settings, printer motion, and material-specific slicing, and the estimate above is not a validated print job.

Use and program

Add water until the percolator arms are covered, checking by eye that every arm sits below the surface. Pack the bowl loosely, light while drawing slowly so the smoke is forced through the slits and breaks into small bubble streams, and continue until the chamber fills. Then lift the bowl and inhale steadily to clear. The program in this record computes the total slit area from the arm count, the slit count, and the slit size, the number of bubble streams, and the water and chamber volumes as cylinders, so the user can check that the diffusion opening matches the specification and that the water level covers the arms. Design-study label: this is a Signature-made product design, presented as a design study only. It is not a real manufactured product, not an established fact, and not a claim that such a product exists or has been tested.

This section gives the closest genuine maker activity for this supply, honestly labelled. A percolator bong cannot be made at home: fusing a tree percolator with hollow slitted arms inside a glass tube is a skilled glassblowing trade, and no home method produces it safely. The closest genuine maker activity is assembling a bought kit and making a cleaning stand for it. Buy a percolator tube, a downstem, and a bowl in matching joint sizes, and check the fit dry before any water goes in: the downstem should seat firmly without wobble, and the water must cover the percolator arms when filled. Then make a drying stand from a block of hardwood: drill a hole the diameter of the tube, cut a slot for the joint, and sand it smooth so the piece rests upright while it drains after cleaning. Test the stand by setting the dry bong in it and pressing the rim gently from the side; it should not rock, and the arms should not touch the wood. Check the fit dry before any water or load goes in, work slowly, and keep the finished piece clean and dry in storage, because a build that is checked at each step is the one that works the first time it is used.

demo.code:
"""Demo: tree percolator slit area and chamber volumes — Signature Grove Tree Perc."""
import hashlib, math
def compute():
    arms = 12; slits = 8; w = 1.2; l = 9.0; d = 65.0; h = 400.0; water_h = 55.0
    slit_area = w * l
    total_slit = arms * slits * slit_area
    streams = arms * slits
    area = math.pi * (d / 2.0) ** 2
    water_mm3 = area * water_h
    chamber_mm3 = area * h
    return {"arms": arms, "slits_per_arm": slits, "slit_area_mm2": round(slit_area, 2), "total_slit_area_mm2": round(total_slit, 2), "bubble_streams": streams, "water_volume_mL": round(water_mm3 / 1000.0, 2), "chamber_volume_mL": round(chamber_mm3 / 1000.0, 2)}
def main():
    a = compute(); b = compute()
    sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    for key in ["arms", "slits_per_arm", "slit_area_mm2", "total_slit_area_mm2", "bubble_streams", "water_volume_mL", "chamber_volume_mL"]:
        print(f"{key}: {a[key]}")
    print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
    print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
    print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The design is sized at 400 mm tall; tube 65 mm diameter; 12-arm tree percolator, each arm 45 mm long with 8 slits; water depth 55 mm, which sets every number in this record, from the volumes and areas in the demo to the scale variants at the end. materials_design: This is a Signature design study, not a real product. Borosilicate glass is chosen for the percolator because the arms must be blown thin and hollow and then cut with slits, and only a glass that tolerates heat and holds a fine edge will keep those slits open and even. The central stem carries the smoke down to the arms, and each arm is a hollow tube open at its slits, so the smoke has nowhere to go but out through the water. The tube wall is made thicker than on a plain bong, because the fused percolator adds weight inside the tube and the piece is handled more during cleaning. Water is the filtration medium, and its level must cover the arms: if an arm sits above the water, its slits pass smoke without diffusing it. The joints are the same ground-glass tapers as on the beaker, 14 mm or 18 mm, sealing by friction with no gasket and no thread. The percolator itself has no joint: it is fused into the tube while the glass is hot, so the arms and the stem are one piece of glass with the tube. The tolerance that matters is the slit size: slits cut too wide pass large bubbles and diffuse poorly, and slits cut too narrow clog quickly and tighten the draw. The downstem seats into the base joint at about 45 degrees, and its tip ends below the water line. The outside is left smooth and clear so the percolator can be seen working and the water level read at a glance. The arms are annealed slowly after they are cut, so the glass around each slit does not hold stress that would crack later. Variants change the arm count, the slit count, and whether a second percolator is stacked above the first, but the tree shape, a central stem with branching arms, stays the same in every version.
math_proof: The demo starts from one slit: a slit 1.2 mm wide and 9.0 mm long has an area of 10.799999999999999 square millimetres. Multiplying by 8 slits per arm and 12 arms gives the total slit area, and the number of bubble streams is the arm count times the slit count, which is 96 streams. The water and chamber volumes are cylinders: pi times the tube radius squared, with a tube diameter of 65.0 mm, times the water depth of 55.0 mm for the water and times the full height of 400.0 mm for the chamber, both reported in millilitres. All numbers come from the specification in this record, and the program prints each result with its unit so the reader can repeat the arithmetic. The reader can check every step with a pocket calculator, because each input is named, each unit is stated, and no hidden constant is used anywhere in the calculation. The computation is run twice and the SHA-256 digests of both runs are printed, confirming the result is deterministic.
method: The method in this record is to describe the supply from its parts, its dimensions, and its mechanism, and then to check those claims with arithmetic and a runnable program. First the parts are named and their materials given, so the reader knows what is metal, what is glass, and what is paper. Then the dimensions are stated in millimetres, grams, watts, or litres, so every later number has a source. Then the mechanism is explained step by step, in the order the user actually follows it, so the reader can picture the motion or the flow. The science proof explains the physics behind that mechanism, and the math proof works the arithmetic from the stated dimensions. Finally the demo program computes the same quantities from the same numbers, prints them with units, and runs twice with SHA-256 digests, so the reader can repeat the whole check on their own machine without trusting this record on faith.
print3d: As a design study, the Signature Grove Tree Perc has not been printed or built; the directions below are for the printable accessory for the public form, adapted to the Signature dimensions. Home 3D printing cannot make every supply in this database, and this section says plainly where the limit falls. A glass percolator bong is not 3D-printable at home: no home filament prints glass, and a printed plastic tube could not hold the fused tree percolator or seal to a glass downstem. The printable accessory is a drying stand and a slit-cleaning pick holder for the piece. Print the stand in PETG, which tolerates warm water and does not crack as easily as PLA, with a 0.4 mm nozzle, 0.2 mm layer height, 4 perimeters, and 25 percent gyroid infill, and print the pick holder in the same material with a snap-fit lid. Print the stand flat on its bottom face with no supports, so the tube hole prints cleanly, and print the holder upright with a brim. Print time (estimate): 2 hours 50 minutes for the stand and 45 minutes for the holder, at the settings given. Unmodelled factors that change real print time and strength are wall thickness, supports, nozzle settings, printer motion, and material-specific slicing: a different slicer profile, a slower first layer, or a damp filament spool will change the result, and the estimate above is not a validated print job. Check the finished accessory against the piece it serves before use, and reprint it if the fit is loose, because a holder that does not grip is worse than no holder at all.
problem: The problem this supply solves is practical and narrow: percolator bong (tree/arm) needs to be prepared or used evenly, reliably, and with ordinary tools, without waste and without guesswork. Before a standard form existed, users improvised, and the result was uneven preparation, spilled material, and parts that wore out or broke. A good supply therefore has to do three things at once: hold the material securely, apply its mechanism evenly across the whole load, and survive repeated use without losing its shape or its edge. It also has to be easy to clean, because residue builds up and changes how it works, and easy to measure, because its dimensions set its capacity. This record states the problem in those terms so the specification, the science proof, and the mathematics can each be checked against it, and so a reader can judge whether the design in the record actually answers the problem it claims to solve.

"""Signature Grove Tree Perc — full working program.

Computes the same quantities as the record demo (tree percolator slit area and chamber volumes),
as a documented module with a class and a run() method.
Run: python3 program.py
"""
import hashlib
import math


class SupplyCalculator:
    """Calculator for Signature Grove Tree Perc."""

    def compute(self):
        """Return the computed quantities as a dict."""
        arms = 12; slits = 8; w = 1.2; l = 9.0; d = 65.0; h = 400.0; water_h = 55.0
        slit_area = w * l
        total_slit = arms * slits * slit_area
        streams = arms * slits
        area = math.pi * (d / 2.0) ** 2
        water_mm3 = area * water_h
        chamber_mm3 = area * h
        return {"arms": arms, "slits_per_arm": slits, "slit_area_mm2": round(slit_area, 2), "total_slit_area_mm2": round(total_slit, 2), "bubble_streams": streams, "water_volume_mL": round(water_mm3 / 1000.0, 2), "chamber_volume_mL": round(chamber_mm3 / 1000.0, 2)}

    def run(self):
        """Compute twice, print named results and SHA-256 digests."""
        a = self.compute()
        b = self.compute()
        sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
        sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
        for key in sorted(a):
            print(f"{key}: {a[key]}")
        print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
        print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
        print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    SupplyCalculator().run()

science_proof: The tree percolator works by diffusion, which is the splitting of one flow into many small flows. Smoke enters the central stem and is forced out through the slits in each hollow arm, so instead of one large bubble rising from the downstem, dozens of small bubbles rise at once from every arm. A small bubble has more surface area for its volume than a large one, so more of the smoke touches water, and more heat passes into the water before the bubble reaches the surface. The total slit area sets how easily smoke gets out: eight arms with six slits each give forty-eight streams, and the sum of the slit areas is the opening the smoke must pass through. If the slits clog with resin, the opening shrinks, the draw tightens, and the diffusion falls, which is why tree percs must be cleaned often. The arms are fragile because they are thin hollow glass with slits cut into them, and a knock that a plain tube would survive can snap an arm. The percolator sits above the base water so the smoke is diffused twice: once at the downstem and once at the arms. The numbers in the specification can be checked against this physics: measure the parts, apply the formulas in the math proof, and run the demo program, and the results should agree within the rounding the program reports. If they do not agree, the measurement or the arithmetic is wrong, not the physics, and the reader can find the error by checking one step at a time.
skeptical_analysis: A careful reader should ask what this record does not prove. It does not prove that every example of this supply matches the dimensions given here, because makers vary sizes, materials, and tolerances, and the numbers in this record describe a common example drawn from the cited sources. It does not prove that the supply performs the same way in every hand, because packing, temperature, and technique change the result, and the record describes the mechanism, not a guarantee of outcome. It makes no claim about health, safety, or benefit, and it gives no advice about how much of anything to use. The science proof explains the physics of the mechanism, not a verdict on the practice, and the mathematics checks internal consistency, not real-world performance. Readers should treat the record as a documented, sourced description with a working calculation, check the cited sources themselves, measure any real object they hold, and follow local law. That is the honest limit of what a reference record can claim.
